newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE construction firms work with new labour law.
newsitem.headline: UAE construction firms work with new labour law.

text.p: The expulsion of illegal workers from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) will affect the country's $6 billion a year construction industry but the move was welcomed on Wednesday by an industry spokesman.

As many as 200,000 illegal workers, many manual workers from the Indian subcontinent and Asia, are scrambling to leave the oil-rich UAE ahead of a government amnesty that gives them till October 31 to get their papers in order or get out.

"The exodus of labour will certainly affect the contracting community. The current amnesty to overstaying and illegal residents will shrink the floating labour market," Ahmed bin Saif Belhasa, chairman of UAE Contractors' Association said.
The association has broadly welcomed the government's decision as it would give legitimate workers more employment rights and reduce workers absconding to other sites.
"The new law is good for both the employee and the employer...(workers) will be fully protected by law...Companies will be able to adjust to the new situation," Belhasa said.
The government has said scores of foreign workers without proper residency forms or employer sponsorship posed a threat to the country's security.
Construction firms which carry out public programmes, road building and office and residential work, employ approximately a total of 400,000 of the country's 1.3 million workforce.
The sector, which has boomed since the end of the 1990-1991 Gulf War, contributes about 14 percent to the UAE's oil-dominated gross domestic product.
An average of 5,000 amnesty seekers, many working in the construction and commerce, are leaving Dubai airport each day.
Managers at private construction firms in the UAE told Reuters the law had left some firms, particularly subcontractors, stripped of their workforce forcing them to suspend building work.

Some were concerned that a tighter labour market could increase wage costs. A typical monthly salary for a construction worker has ranged between 400 and 800 UAE dirhams a month ($108-217), a level that made creating cities in the desert viable.
"Companies which often hire labour from the floating labour market will face a temporary problem," Belhasa said.

International and large-scale Gulf contruction firms based in Dubai have also given their support to the new employment law, saying it would discourage illegal hiring and regulate employment conditions.
